introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 2 c) : altitudes (Mount Cameroon environ 4 000 m, Manengouba environ 2 400 m, Bamboutos environ 2 700 m, Oku environ 3 000 m) et exemples (lacs de cratère de Manengouba, Oku, Nyos, Monoun, Barombi Mbo ; plaine de Ndop ; chutes de Menchum) cités de mémoire avec « about » ; reconnus mais à vérifier. Le détail des escarpements (Ring Road, bassin de Mamfe) est présenté avec prudence.

Question 2 a) : formulation « Describe and explain TWO major landforms » : dorsale médio-océanique et rift continental retenus ; d'autres choix (volcans boucliers, plateaux basaltiques, îles volcaniques) sont mentionnés à la fin du corrigé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) de trois sous-questions : codées « a », « b », « c » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b », « OR-c » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Sujet scanné de cinq pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de planche de carte topographique 1:50 000 « Dufftown » avec ses signes conventionnels, puis le fond de carte du Cameroun pour la question 3c i). Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2024, Three Hours. Filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés. La planche topographique (page 4) appartient aux épreuves de cartographie (Paper 3) et ne sert à aucune question de ce Paper 2 : non transcrite. Seul le fond de carte du Cameroun (page 5) est utilisé (question 3).

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 8+8+9, Q2 6+10+9, Q3 8+8+(3+6=9), Q4 6+10+9, Q5 5+9+11, Q6 8+9+8, Q7 EITHER 9+8+8, OR 6+10+9). Aucun écart avec le sujet. Le sujet imprime des marks pour un ensemble de sous-points (ex. Q1 a (i)+(ii) = 8 marks) : le corrigé les regroupe sous une seule sous-question.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Describe and explain **TWO** major landforms produced at constructive margins.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
At a **constructive (divergent) plate margin** two plates move apart; the gap is filled by magma that rises from the mantle and cools to form new crust. Two landforms are described and explained (3 marks each).

**1. Mid-ocean ridge (for example the Mid-Atlantic Ridge).**
- *Description:* a continuous submarine mountain chain, thousands of kilometres long, rising 2 to 3 km above the ocean floor, with a central rift valley along its crest, offset by many transform faults; in places the ridge rises above the sea (Iceland, the Azores, Ascension).
- *Explanation:* where two oceanic plates diverge (driven by mantle convection, ridge push and slab pull), the pressure falls and the hot mantle rock partly melts (decompression melting). Basaltic magma rises into the gap, cools and forms new oceanic crust; fresh, hot crust is less dense, so it stands higher. The new crust is carried away on each side, so the ridge is symmetrical, and the rocks are older away from the ridge (shown by symmetrical bands of magnetic reversal). Repeated eruptions build up a chain of volcanoes and basalt lava pillows.

**2. Rift valley (for example the East African Rift Valley).**
- *Description:* a long, narrow, steep-sided trough on the continent, bounded by parallel faults, with a flat floor that contains lakes (Lake Tanganyika, Lake Malawi) and volcanoes along the floor and edges (for example Nyiragongo).
- *Explanation:* where a continental plate is pulled apart, the crust is stretched and thinned, and it breaks along parallel **normal faults**; the central block between them drops down (a **graben**) while the sides remain as high scarps (horsts). Hot mantle rock rises under the thinned crust, uplifting the area, and magma reaches the surface to form volcanoes. If the process continues, the rift may widen and open into a new ocean (as in the Red Sea).

(Other landforms that could be chosen: shield volcanoes and basalt plateaus, fissure eruptions, and volcanic islands such as Iceland.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Briefly describe any **TWO** major hazards associated with weathering and suggest any two measures that can be used to cope with the hazards.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Weathering** is the breakdown of rock in place. It makes slopes and ground weak and it damages structures. Two hazards are described, each with two measures (5 marks each: about 2 for description and 3 for measures).

**Hazard 1: Landslides, rockfalls and other mass movements on weathered slopes.**
*Description:* physical weathering (frost action, heating and cooling) opens joints and cracks; in the humid tropics, chemical weathering turns rock into a thick, weak layer of regolith. When heavy rain saturates this material, or the base of the slope is cut away, it moves downslope. This kills people and destroys houses, roads and farms; it is a serious hazard on the steep, built-up slopes of towns such as Limbe, Bamenda and Buea.
*Measures:*
1. **Land-use control and slope protection:** forbid or restrict building on steep and unstable slopes (zoning), and keep or plant a cover of deep-rooted vegetation and trees (afforestation) and terraces that bind the soil and reduce overland flow.
2. **Engineering and drainage:** retaining walls, drains and gutters that remove surface water, rock bolting and wire netting on rock faces, and regrading of slopes to a gentler angle; with monitoring and early warning, and evacuation of residents at risk.

**Hazard 2: Ground subsidence, sinkholes and damage to buildings and infrastructure.**
*Description:* in limestone areas, carbonation and solution widen joints into caves and sinkholes whose roofs can collapse suddenly; in clay soils, weathering produces clay that swells when wet and shrinks when dry, so that foundations and walls crack; salt weathering and acid rain crumble stone, concrete and monuments, and in cold areas frost action breaks roads (potholes) and walls. The cost is repairs and the loss of property.
*Measures:*
1. **Careful site selection and design:** surveys before building, deep or reinforced foundations, and flexible joints; avoid building on cavernous limestone and on expanding clays; good drainage so that water does not accumulate under buildings.
2. **Protection and maintenance:** use of resistant materials and protective coatings or sealants, waterproofing, filling and grouting of sinkholes, regular inspection and repair, and reduction of air pollution that causes acid rain.

(Other hazards that could be chosen: damage to historic monuments, loss of soil fertility by the deep leaching of tropical soils, and rock debris on roads.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Show how the relief of the Western Highlands is characterized by a diversity of landforms.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Western Highlands of Cameroon** (the Bamenda Highlands, the Bamileke and Bamoun plateaus and the volcanic mountains) form a high, rugged region in the west of the country, between about 1,000 m and more than 3,000 m. They are part of the **Cameroon Volcanic Line**, a chain of volcanoes and uplifted blocks that runs from the Gulf of Guinea to the north-east, built on a very old basement of granite and gneiss. The mixture of volcanic activity, faulting, uplift and erosion has produced a **great diversity of landforms**.

**1. High volcanic mountains and cones.** Mount Cameroon (about 4,000 m, the highest peak of the region and an active volcano), Mount Manengouba (about 2,400 m), the Bamboutos mountains (about 2,700 m) and Mount Oku (about 3,000 m, the highest peak of the Bamenda Highlands) are volcanic massifs with steep slopes, built of basaltic and trachytic lavas and ash; many have **calderas and cinder cones** on their flanks.

**2. Crater lakes.** Water has filled volcanic craters and calderas to form crater lakes, for example the twin lakes on Manengouba, Lake Oku, Lake Nyos and Lake Monoun (famous for the gas disasters of the 1980s), and Barombi Mbo near Kumba.

**3. Lava plateaus.** Wide, flat to gently undulating surfaces built up by successive lava flows or uplifted, at about 1,000 to 2,000 m, such as the Bamenda plateau, the Bamileke plateau and the Bamoun plateau; they are dissected by rivers into deep valleys and ridges, and the lava flows have formed basalt sheets and ridges.

**4. Escarpments and fault scarps.** The edges of the plateaus are steep faulted or eroded slopes (for example the scarp that falls from the Bamenda highlands to the lowlands of the Mamfe basin), with waterfalls where rivers plunge over resistant rock.

**5. Granite domes, inselbergs and rocky outcrops.** Where the basement granite is exposed, weathering has left bare rock domes and rounded hills (bornhardts), and tors with blocks of boulders.

**6. Basins and plains.** Between the mountains there are flat areas filled by volcanic and alluvial deposits, with swampy lake-bed plains such as the **Ndop plain** and valley floors of the rivers (the Noun, the Mbam, the Katsina-Ala and the Cross River basin).

**7. River landforms.** Streams radiate from the volcanic summits, cutting V-shaped valleys, gorges and waterfalls (for example the Menchum Falls), and the plains show meanders and flood plains.

A **sketch map** or a block diagram showing the Cameroon Volcanic Line, the main mountains (Mount Cameroon, Manengouba, Bamboutos, Oku), the plateaus and the Ndop plain would earn marks for annotation.

**Conclusion:** the region is characterised by an unusual variety of landforms: high volcanic cones and calderas, crater lakes, lava plateaus, fault scarps, granite domes and basins. The result is a variety of climates, soils and land use over short distances.
